warmup.q: The payments app keeps its payments on three machines, split by the time each payment was made: each machine owns one stretch of time. A program that evens the machines out has made sure each holds about a third of the payments. At 09:00 the morning rush starts, 3,000 new payments a second. How are those new payments spread?
options: About 1,000 a second on each machine, because each holds a third
All 3,000 on one machine, the one that owns the latest stretch of time
Handed to each machine in turn, then moved to the right one later
Evenly, because the database scrambles the times before it splits them
warmup.why: An even split describes the payments already stored. Each machine owns a stretch of time, and every new payment is later than all the others, so every one falls in the latest stretch, and one machine owns it. The program that evens things out can move old stretches away afterwards, but at 09:00 one machine takes all 3,000 writes, like the third attendant in the cloakroom. MongoDB scrambles the key first only when you ask it to (a hashed key, which this lesson meets later), and it never hands writes out in turn: each one goes straight to the machine that owns its key.

sections.h: One MongoDB server, and the log its copies replay
sections.html:
Let's start with one machine and grow it. MongoDB (version 9.0 in this lesson) keeps each record as a document, a set of named fields such as { _id: "pay-81723", amountMinor: 4250, status: "AUTHORIZED" }. Every document has an _id, its unique name. Payments live together in a collection, MongoDB's word for a table.

A MongoDB server is one running program, mongod. It listens for clients on port 27017, the number that tells a machine which program a network message is for, and keeps its files in one folder. Inside, its storage engine, WiredTiger, keeps each collection as a B-tree: a sorted tree of small blocks, called pages, that finds any key in a few steps. Each index, a sorted list that finds documents by one field, is a B-tree too. Pages in use stay in a cache in memory. Every 60 seconds WiredTiger writes a checkpoint, a consistent snapshot of its files. In between, each change goes first to a journal, a file that changes are appended to, so a crash loses nothing the journal has.

One machine still has one weakness: when it dies, card payments stop. So we keep copies. Picture the cloakroom before the split. One attendant writes every coat in and out in a notebook, and two assistants copy each line, so either can take over if he faints.

MongoDB's version is a replica set: a group of mongod servers that hold the same data. One of them, the primary, takes every write. The others, the secondaries, copy it. The primary's notebook is the oplog (operations log), a collection named local.oplog.rs. Each write adds one entry, which usually describes a change to one document, and secondaries fetch the entries and apply them in the same order. The oplog is a capped collection: it has a fixed size, keeps entries in the order they came, and drops the oldest when it's full.

One rule makes the copying safe. Applying an entry twice must give the same result as applying it once, which is called being idempotent. Say a payment holds 42.50 and the app asks to add 1.00 to it ($inc: { amountMinor: 100 }, with amounts in cents). "Add 100", applied twice, would give 44.50. So the primary doesn't record what you asked for. It records what came out: amountMinor: 4350, "the amount is now 43.50". A secondary that crashes halfway through a batch of entries can apply the whole batch again and end in the same state. The Try-it shows the rewrite.

The oplog's size decides how long a secondary may be away. By default it's 5% of the free disk, at least 990 MB and at most 50 GB. The time between its oldest and newest entry is the oplog window. A secondary that comes back within the window replays what it missed. One that was away longer finds that the entries it needs were dropped. It must copy every document again, an initial sync, and for 2 TB of payments that can take most of a day. At 2 GB of oplog an hour, a 50 GB oplog holds 25 hours. If a member may be down for a long weekend, make the oplog bigger with replSetResizeOplog, or set a minimum in hours with oplogMinRetentionHours.

A replica set is MongoDB's building block. A primary orders the writes; secondaries replay them. Next, we'll set one up, and see how the secondaries choose a new primary when the old one stops answering.

sections.h: Three servers become a replica set and elect a primary
sections.html:
A replica set is set up in two steps. Start every member with the same set name, then tell one of them who the members are:

// each member was started with: mongod --replSet rs0 --bind_ip_all
rs.initiate({ _id: "rs0", members: [
  { _id: 0, host: "mongo1:27017", priority: 2 },
  { _id: 1, host: "mongo2:27017" },
  { _id: 2, host: "mongo3:27017" } ] })

env/mongo-rs.yml runs exactly this. mongo1 stores the member list, the others fetch it, and within seconds they choose a primary. How do three servers agree on which one leads, and what happens when the leader stops answering?

They hold an election. Its rules come from Raft, a well-known method for machines to agree on one leader by majority vote (the Consensus track builds it). Each election has a number, the term, and each member votes at most once per term, so two candidates can't both win the same one. Members send each other a heartbeat, a small "I'm alive" message, every 2 seconds. A secondary that hears nothing from the primary for 10 seconds (electionTimeoutMillis) becomes a candidate. It adds one to the term, votes for itself and asks the others. A member votes only for a candidate whose oplog is at least as recent as its own, so a member that missed writes can't win. Votes from a majority of the voting members, 2 of 3 here, make a new primary. The MongoDB docs say the typical election finishes within 12 seconds.

You can steer elections with settings on each member. A member with a higher priority calls elections sooner and, once it has caught up, takes the primary role back. Priority 0 means it never becomes primary. Two more settings give a member a side job. hidden: true keeps the app's reads away from it, which suits a member used for backups. secondaryDelaySecs: 3600 makes a member apply the oplog an hour late, so if a bad change deletes every payment, it still has them for an hour. It also needs hidden, priority 0 and votes: 0, and its delay must be shorter than the oplog window.

There's also a member that votes and holds no data, the arbiter (arbiterOnly: true). It looks like a cheap third server. Avoid it. Payments are written with w: "majority": MongoDB confirms a write only once a majority of the members have stored it. With a primary, a secondary and an arbiter, lose the secondary and only one member can store anything, so those writes stall. A third member with data costs one more disk, and it's a real copy.

Reads have a setting too, the read preference. The default sends every read to the primary, which has every confirmed write. Other choices spread reads over the secondaries, which lag behind by milliseconds normally and minutes during a network problem. Read a balance from the primary; a month-end statement can come from a secondary.

So far every member holds every payment. Next, we'll see where that stops working.

sections.h: When one replica set is too small: shards, a map and a router
sections.html:
A replica set puts every document on every member, and that gives it two limits. The data must fit on one machine's disk, and the part people read must fit in its cache. A 16 GB server gives its cache about 7.5 GB, so with 3 TB of payments most reads go to disk, which is far slower than memory. And every write goes through one primary. Say it takes 8,000 new payments a second at 70% of its processor, and the busiest shopping day of the year needs 25,000. More secondaries don't help, because each one must replay all 25,000 writes too.

So we split the payments over several replica sets. That's sharding, and each replica set that holds a part is a shard: one cloakroom attendant, with assistants copying his notebook.

Version 1 splits in the app: accounts A-0000 to A-4999 go to set 1, the rest to set 2, a rule in the code. When set 1 fills up, a third set means changing every copy of the program at once, and moving data while payments keep arriving.

Version 2 turns the rule into data: a table of key ranges, and the set that holds each one. That table is now the most important data in the system, so it gets a replica set of its own. The app talks to a router, which keeps a copy of the table in memory and passes each request on. In the cloakroom, the table is a board by the door, and the router is a porter who reads it and sends you to the right counter. That's MongoDB's sharded cluster, in the figure:

  • A shard is a replica set (three members for real use) that holds part of each sharded collection.
  • The config server replica set holds the map, in a database called config. Its config.chunks collection lists every range and the shard that owns it. The balancer, which the last section meets, runs on its primary. If the config servers can't elect a primary, the map can't change: reads and writes go on, but no data moves.
  • mongos is the router. It stores nothing on disk. Apps connect only to mongos, so you run several, often one next to each copy of the app.

A sharded collection has a shard key: a field, or a few fields, of its documents. All the possible values of the key are cut into chunks (the 9.0 docs also call them ranges), and each chunk belongs to one shard. The first chunk starts at MinKey, a special value below every other, and the last ends at MaxKey, above every other. For an insert, mongos reads the document's shard key, finds the chunk whose range holds it, and sends the insert to that shard's primary.

A query whose filter gives the shard key is targeted: mongos asks only the shards that own matching chunks. explain(), which reports how a query ran, says SINGLE_SHARD when that's one. A query without the shard key goes to every shard, and mongos merges the answers. That's a scatter-gather read, SHARD_MERGE in explain(). Each shard indexes only its own documents (the lesson Secondary indexes across shards calls that a local index), so nothing else tells mongos where to look. A scatter-gather read is as slow as the slowest shard, and every shard pays for it.

The worked example has the commands that start each kind of program, and env/mongo-sharded.yml runs them with one member per set, to fit on a laptop. Everything now hangs on the shard key. Next, we'll try a few and see where the new payments land.

sections.h: Choosing the shard key: where new payments land, and which reads ask every shard
sections.html:
In the cloakroom, the ticket number decided which attendant took each coat. Here the shard key does. mongos routes by it alone, so it decides where each new document goes and which reads are targeted. Judge a candidate by three things.

Cardinality is the number of different values a key has. All documents with one value live in one chunk. So a key with 3 values, such as the currency of payments in euros, dollars and pounds, can never use more than 3 shards.

Frequency is how often the most common value turns up. Shard on the shop, merchantId (the labs call shops merchants), and the busiest shop, M-0042, with a fifth of all payments, fills one chunk that grows without limit. A chunk that's bigger than the chunk size and can't be cut, because every document in it has the same key, is a jumbo chunk. The lab makes one.

A monotonic key only ever grows: the time of a payment, a counter, or the ObjectId that MongoDB puts in _id when you don't choose one. Its first 4 bytes are the time it was made. This is the cloakroom's ticket number. Every new value is beyond all the old ones, so every insert goes to the last chunk, the one that ends at MaxKey, on one shard.

Then choose how the key is cut. Ranged sharding cuts the values in their natural order, so neighbours stay together and a query for a range of the key is targeted. Hashed sharding, { _id: "hashed" }, cuts a hash of the value instead. A hash is a number worked out from the value that looks random, so values that are close together get hashes far apart. A growing key's inserts then spread evenly, and a lookup of one value is still targeted, but a range of values is scattered. A key of two fields can mix both. Under { accountId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 }, accounts spread evenly over the shards, and one account's payments sit together in time order.

Now test four candidates against the questions the payments app asks most:

Shard key New payments An account's newest payments One payment by its id A shop's dashboard
{ createdAt: 1 } all on one shard every shard every shard every shard
{ merchantId: 1 } M-0042's shard overloaded; a jumbo chunk every shard every shard one shard
{ _id: "hashed" } even every shard one shard every shard
{ accountId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 } even one shard every shard every shard

Take the last one. The account screen is the busiest read, and there are millions of accounts, each with a few payments a day. The shop dashboard can read a reporting copy fed by a change stream, MongoDB's feed of committed changes.

One more rule follows from the key. A unique index, one that refuses a second document with the same value, works across the whole cluster only if it starts with the shard key. Each shard's index sees only its own documents, so even _id is unique only within each shard when it isn't the shard key. Document stores with MongoDB put a unique index on the idempotency key, a value the app sends again with every retry so a payment can't count twice. In a collection sharded by account, that index can't exist. Keep those keys in a collection of their own, with the key itself as _id and as the shard key.

The stored payments still have to be evened out, though, and sometimes a key has to change. Next, we'll watch the program that moves data between shards.

sections.h: The balancer moves ranges, and bigger tools move whole collections
sections.html:
The ledger from the last Try-it sits on one shard: 20 MB against nothing. No insert will fix that. Before MongoDB 6.0.3, a shard cut a chunk in two once it grew past the chunk size, 128 MB by default. Since 6.0.3, inserts never cut a chunk, though sh.status() still says autosplit is enabled. The balancer looks at data size instead. When the shard with the most of a collection and the one with the least differ by three chunk sizes (384 MB at the default), it moves a range. It cuts about one chunk size off a big chunk as it goes. In the cloakroom, it's a supervisor who wheels a rail of coats from the busiest attendant to the quietest, then changes the board.

The cloakroom picture breaks here. Nobody hangs coats on a rail while it's being wheeled away, but MongoDB keeps the range open for writes almost the whole time. The stepper walks through one move, called a migration. The balancer sends moveRange to the donor, the shard giving the range away. The recipient builds the collection's indexes and copies the documents while the donor still takes the range's writes. Then the recipient catches up on the changes made during the copy. The donor pauses writes to the range for a moment and records the new owner in config.chunks.

The donor's old copies stay on disk as orphans, documents a shard holds but no longer owns, until no read in progress needs them. Each shard takes part in one migration at a time. And the porter's copy of the board is now out of date. If mongos asks the old owner, that shard answers StaleConfig, and mongos fetches the new map and asks again.

A jumbo chunk can't be cut, and the balancer won't move a chunk that's too big. moveRange with forceJumbo: true can, but it blocks writes to the collection for the whole move. The cure is a better key. refineCollectionShardKey adds fields to the end of the key, so { merchantId: 1, createdAt: 1 } lets M-0042's chunk be cut by time. reshardCollection (5.0 and later) rebuilds the collection under a new key. Each shard copies the documents it will own and replays the changes made meanwhile. When less than 500 ms of work is left, writes pause and the new key takes effect. That needs room for a second copy, and time in proportion to the data.

MongoDB 8.0 added moves for whole collections, and 9.0 keeps them. A collection that isn't sharded lives on one shard, at first its database's primary shard (the shard the database started on), so small collections pile up there. moveCollection moves one to another shard without sharding it. unshardCollection brings a sharded collection back onto one shard. And reshardCollection to the same key now rebalances faster, because every shard copies its new share at once. All three copy, catch up, then switch over, and the Try-it shows their floor: at least 5 minutes by default, even for a tiny collection.

Balanced data isn't balanced work. Check where the next write goes. The stepper ends on exactly that, and Go deeper has a checklist for a real cluster.

steps: In the same shell, paste the block. Its first half sets the ledger's chunk size to 1 MB, the smallest allowed, and waits 30 seconds. Predict how many ranges move, from which end of the time line, and where the next 1,000 entries go.

Its second half moves a whole collection, the 8.0 way. It shortens the 5-minute floor on the lab's config server (a shortcut for the lab only), makes a merchants collection that isn't sharded and moves it to shard2. Predict which shard holds it first. moveCollection takes about half a minute.

opening:
Picture a theatre cloakroom with three attendants. They split the work by ticket number: the first takes tickets 1 to 300, the second 301 to 600, the third everything from 601 up. By the interval, each one holds about 300 coats.

Then the late crowd arrives. Tickets go out in order, so every new coat has a higher number than all the others, and every one goes to the third attendant. Two stand idle while one runs.

The payments app can fall into the same trap. Its payments no longer fit on one machine, so a team splits them over three by time. A screen says each holds a third, which sounds like a third of the work each. But it counts the coats already hung up, not the queue.

In Setting up and running a Cassandra cluster, data moved only when a person typed a command. MongoDB, a free database program, moves it by itself. In this lesson, we'll grow a MongoDB cluster from one server, then choose a key that spreads the work. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a cloakroom whose work was split fairly by ticket number, until every new coat went to the last attendant. A payments collection sharded on time does the same: the balancer evens out yesterday's payments, and every new one lands on one shard.

If you ever use a sharded MongoDB, run sh.status() and find the chunk that ends at MaxKey. Then ask what the next document's shard key will be, and which chunk it will fall in.

Next, we'll open up DynamoDB, a database that Amazon runs for you, and ask what happens when one key gets more writes than any one of its machines will take.

worked.title: Set up a sharded payments cluster, from programs to a checked shard key

steps.say: Start the programs: three members for the config servers, three for each shard, and one mongos on each machine that runs the payments app. Every member of one replica set gets the same --replSet name.
steps.code: # config server replica set (on cfg1, cfg2, cfg3) mongod --configsvr --replSet cfg --port 27019 --bind_ip_all --dbpath /data/cfg # shard replica sets (on sh1a, sh1b, sh1c and sh2a, sh2b, sh2c) mongod --shardsvr --replSet shard1 --port 27018 --bind_ip_all --dbpath /data/db # routers, next to the payment service mongos --configdb cfg/cfg1:27019,cfg2:27019,cfg3:27019 --port 27017 --bind_ip_all

steps.say: Set up each replica set from one of its members. Every shard looks the same; configsvr: true marks the config servers.
steps.code: // on cfg1 rs.initiate({ _id: "cfg", configsvr: true, members: [ { _id: 0, host: "cfg1:27019" }, { _id: 1, host: "cfg2:27019" }, { _id: 2, host: "cfg3:27019" } ] }) // on sh1a (and the same for shard2 on sh2a) rs.initiate({ _id: "shard1", members: [ { _id: 0, host: "sh1a:27018" }, { _id: 1, host: "sh1b:27018" }, { _id: 2, host: "sh1c:27018" } ] })

steps.say: On a mongos, add the shards, then shard payments on the key the table in the fourth section chose. On an empty collection MongoDB builds the shard key's index itself and, for a hashed first field, makes one chunk per shard.
steps.code: sh.addShard("shard1/sh1a:27018,sh1b:27018,sh1c:27018") sh.addShard("shard2/sh2a:27018,sh2b:27018,sh2c:27018") sh.shardCollection("sfz.payments", { accountId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 })

steps.say: A unique value that isn't the shard key gets a collection of its own. The idempotency key is each claim's _id and its shard key, so a duplicate fails on whichever shard owns it. A TTL index (time to live) deletes each claim once its expiresAt time has passed.

steps.say: Check the result before traffic arrives: the shards, the chunks, and that the account screen's query goes to one shard. If migrations slow the busiest hours, give the balancer a window to work in.
steps.code: sh.status() db.payments.getShardDistribution() db.payments.find({ accountId: "A-1001" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(20).explain().queryPlanner.winningPlan.stage // SINGLE_SHARD: one account's payments live on one shard, in time order // optional: keep migrations out of the peak db.getSiblingDB("config").settings.updateOne({ _id: "balancer" }, { $set: { activeWindow: { start: "23:00", stop: "05:00" } } }, { upsert: true })

In ShardedCluster.kt, the constructor already shards an empty collection the way MongoDB 8.0 and later do: one chunk per shard for a hashed first field, one chunk on the first shard for a ranged key. Write chunkFor and insert. The chunkFor and hashed-spread tests pass: 30,000 payments land between 9,500 and 10,500 per shard.

hints: chunks.floorEntry(key).value finds the chunk for a key. The chunks cover MinKey to MaxKey with no gaps, so there is always one. Key is Comparable, so <= and > work on keys.
A chunk [min, max) overlaps the range [lo, hi] (both ends included) when min <= range.hi && max > range.lo.
Runs of equal keys: walk chunk.keys.sorted() and start a new run whenever the key differs from the current run's first key.

Packing runs into pieces: if (current != null && (current.size + run.size).toLong() * docBytes <= chunkSizeBytes) current += run else pieces += ArrayList(run). Then remove the old chunk by its min and put each piece under its own min. Iterate over chunks.values.toList() so you don't change the map while walking it.

Pairing shards: sort once with compareByDescending<String> { bytes.getValue(it) }.thenBy { shards.indexOf(it) }, then walk inwards from both ends. chunks.values.firstOrNull { it.shard == from && !it.jumbo } is the donor's chunk with the smallest min, because a TreeMap iterates in key order.

drill.title: A replica set and a sharded collection, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the rs.initiate for a set rs0 where mongo1 is the preferred primary and mongo3 is a hidden copy that runs an hour behind and doesn't vote. Then write the commands, run on mongos, that add one shard shard1 (members sh1a, sh1b and sh1c on port 27018) and shard sfz.payments so that new payments spread and an account's newest payments are one targeted query. Add one line each: why no arbiter, and why not { createdAt: 1 }.

answer.html: rs.initiate({ _id: "rs0", members: [ { _id: 0, host: "mongo1:27017", priority: 2 }, // preferred primary { _id: 1, host: "mongo2:27017" }, { _id: 2, host: "mongo3:27017", priority: 0, hidden: true, // never primary, never read secondaryDelaySecs: 3600, votes: 0 } ] }) // an hour behind, no vote sh.addShard("shard1/sh1a:27018,sh1b:27018,sh1c:27018") sh.shardCollection("sfz.payments", { accountId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 }) // no arbiter: it holds no data, so losing one data member leaves a single copy // and w: "majority" writes stall; a third data-bearing member is a real copy // not { createdAt: 1 }: every insert is later than all others, so all of them // go to the chunk ending at MaxKey, on one shard

recap: A MongoDB server, mongod, keeps each collection and index as a B-tree in its storage engine, WiredTiger, with a cache in memory, a checkpoint every 60 seconds and a journal in between, so a crash loses nothing the journal has.

A replica set is a primary and its secondaries. The primary records each write in its oplog as a result, never as an instruction like "add 100", so replaying an entry twice is safe. The oplog window is how long a secondary may be away and still catch up without copying everything again.

Members elect a primary by majority vote: heartbeats every 2 seconds, a candidate after 10 seconds of silence, one vote per term, and only for a candidate whose oplog is at least as recent. Priorities pick the preferred primary, and an arbiter, a member with a vote and no data, is a false saving.

A sharded cluster is shards (each a replica set), a config server replica set that holds the chunk map and runs the balancer, and mongos routers that store nothing. A query with the shard key goes to one shard (SINGLE_SHARD); one without it asks every shard (SHARD_MERGE).

Choose a shard key with many values, no value that dominates and no steady growth, which the busiest queries include. A key that only grows sends every insert to the chunk that ends at MaxKey, a dominant value makes a jumbo chunk, and a unique index must start with the shard key.

The limit: the balancer evens out the data already stored, never where the next write goes, and a bad key is fixed only by copying the whole collection again with reshardCollection. Since 8.0, moveCollection and unshardCollection move whole collections the same way, in at least 5 minutes each by default.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to shard the payments collection on { createdAt: 1 }, because "every report filters by date, and sh.status() will show the data balanced". Explain what happens to new payments, what the balancer does about it, and which key you'd use instead.
explain.answer: A ranged key keeps values in order, and each chunk owns one range. Every new payment has a later createdAt than all the others, so every insert lands in the last chunk, the one that ends at MaxKey, and that chunk lives on one shard. That shard's primary takes every write while the others sit idle. The balancer only looks at stored data. When the shards differ by three chunk sizes, it moves old ranges off the full shard, so sh.status() does look balanced, but the newest range never leaves, and the busy shard stays busy. In the Try-it, after eight migrations, the next 1,000 entries still all went to shard1. Reports that filter by date are a weak reason anyway: they can ask every shard, or run on a reporting copy. For the payments app I'd use { accountId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 }. The hash spreads the millions of accounts evenly, so new payments spread, and one account's payments stay together in time order, so the account screen, the busiest read, asks one shard. Idempotency keys go in a collection of their own, keyed by the idempotency key, because a unique index must start with the shard key.

deeper.html:
Most of a cluster's safety is decided before the first payment arrives. Check these before a real cluster takes payments:

  • three members with data in every replica set, in three separate places that don't fail together (racks, the cabinets machines sit in, or data centres), and no arbiters;
  • w: "majority" for payments, and reads from the primary for decisions;
  • an oplog window longer than your longest planned outage, watched with rs.printReplicationInfo();
  • sharding only once one replica set can't hold the data or take the writes;
  • a shard key with many values, no dominant value and no steady growth, which your busiest queries include (analyzeShardKey, in 7.0 and later, scores a candidate from sampled queries);
  • a config server replica set of three members, and several mongos near the app;
  • unique indexes that start with the shard key;
  • a balancer window (activeWindow) if migrations slow your busiest hours.

Some sizes and small print. A replica set can have up to 50 members, at most 7 of them voting, and since 5.3 MongoDB refuses a second arbiter unless you set allowMultipleArbiters. WiredTiger's cache is, by default, the larger of half of (the memory minus 1 GB) and 256 MB, so a 16 GB server gives it 7.5 GB. Since 6.0 you don't need sh.enableSharding() before sh.shardCollection(), which creates whatever is missing. Orphans still count in getShardDistribution() until the donor deletes them.

Zones pin key ranges to shards. With sh.addShardToZone("shard1", "EU") and a matching sh.updateZoneKeyRange, the balancer keeps European accounts on European machines.

A read preference can carry maxStalenessSeconds (90 at least), which tells the driver to skip any secondary that has fallen further behind than that.

Elections have one more dial. A newly elected primary can spend up to catchUpTimeoutMillis copying newer writes from other members it can reach before it starts taking writes. That saves some writes confirmed by the primary alone (w: 1) from being rolled back, undone when the old primary rejoins, at the cost of a slower failover. MongoDB's election protocol, protocol version 1, promises to keep writes confirmed with w: "majority"; anything less is a matter of luck and timing, as the failure at the end of Document stores with MongoDB showed. Zhou and Mu's NSDI 2021 paper describes the protocol as derived from Raft, with one big difference: secondaries pull the oplog from a sync source, which can be another secondary, instead of the primary pushing to every follower. That's why a set spread over two data centres can have the far secondaries copy from each other and send one stream across the link.

MongoDB 8.0 also added config shards: the config server replica set can store app data too, which saves a replica set in a small cluster (sh.isConfigShardEnabled() tells you).

Orphans matter for reads too. A shard still holding orphans filters them out with a SHARDING_FILTER stage at the top of each shard's plan in explain(). Reads with read concern available (a read setting that takes whatever a shard holds, for speed) skip that filter and can return orphans, one more reason to leave read concern at its default for payments.

Last, the AutoMerger joins neighbouring chunks that sit on the same shard, so the number of chunks doesn't grow for ever as migrations cut ranges.
